history.heading: Inuit and Norse
paragraphs: Greenland, the world's largest island, has been settled in several waves by peoples from North America, beginning around 4,500 years ago. The ancestors of today's Inuit, the Thule people, arrived around 1200 CE.
Norse settlers led by Erik the Red established colonies in southern Greenland around 985, but these were abandoned by the 15th century, possibly due to a cooling climate and isolation.

history.heading: Danish colonisation
paragraphs: The Norwegian-Danish missionary Hans Egede arrived in 1721, beginning Danish colonisation. Greenland remained a Danish colony, closed to most outsiders, until 1953, when it became an integral part of Denmark.

During the Second World War, the United States established bases in Greenland, and it still operates the Pituffik Space Base. Greenland gained home rule in 1979 and self-government in 2009, recognising Greenlanders as a people with the right to self-determination. In 2025 US statements about acquiring Greenland caused tensions with Greenland and Denmark.

culture.heading: Inuit culture
paragraphs: About 90 percent of the roughly 56,000 inhabitants are Inuit. Greenlandic (Kalaallisut) is the official language, and Danish is also widely used. Most people are Lutheran.
Traditional culture includes kayaks (an Inuit invention), dog sledding, drum dancing and carving. Seal, whale, fish and musk ox are traditional foods. Greenland's national day is 21 June.

politics.heading: Self-government
paragraphs: Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark with its own parliament (Inatsisartut) and government (Naalakkersuisut), which control most domestic matters, including natural resources. Denmark handles defence, foreign policy and currency, and provides a large annual block grant.
Most political parties favour eventual independence, though they differ on timing. Greenland left the European Community in 1985 over fishing rights.

economy.heading: Fishing and resources
paragraphs: Fishing, especially shrimp and halibut, accounts for most exports. The Danish block grant funds a large part of public spending. Greenland has deposits of rare earths, uranium, zinc, gold and other minerals, which have attracted international interest, though uranium mining was banned in 2021.
Tourism is growing, helped by new international airports. Climate change is melting the ice sheet, affecting traditional ways of life. The currency is the Danish krone.
